chapterTitle: Inheritance and Polymorphism in Unreal Engine
aiGenerationNote:
Develop a 10-minute video tutorial. Begin with a conceptual explanation of inheritance using a clear class hierarchy diagram (e.g., `AActor` -> `APawn` -> `ACharacter` -> `AMyPlayerCharacter`). Then, transition to a live coding demo in Unreal Engine. Show how to create a base `AEnemy` class with a virtual `Attack()` function. Subsequently, create two derived classes, `AZombieEnemy` and `ASpiderEnemy`, each overriding the `Attack()` function with unique console log messages. Conclude by demonstrating polymorphism: create an `AActor` that spawns both `AZombieEnemy` and `ASpiderEnemy` objects, stores them in a `TArray<AEnemy*>`, and then iterates through the array, calling `Attack()` on each. Show the different log messages appearing in the output log. Include an interactive element where the learner modifies the `Attack()` message for one of the derived classes.

---

screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism in Unreal Engine
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll see how inheritance and polymorphism form the backbone of extendable game systems in Unreal Engine. We use inheritance to express “is-a” relationships: a zombie is an enemy, a character is an actor. That gives derived types automatic access to fields and behaviors defined in a base class, reducing duplication and organizing code. Polymorphism lets code treat many concrete types through a single interface. Using virtual functions, the engine will call the appropriate derived implementation at runtime, so a single loop over an array of base-class pointers triggers zombie attacks, spider bites, or dragon fire without explicit type checks. You will also learn the difference between virtual and pure virtual functions, why an abstract base class enforces an interface, and why the override keyword prevents subtle bugs. Practical examples in this chapter build an AWeapon base class and ARifle/APistol derived classes, plus a WeaponManager that demonstrates calling Fire() polymorphically. By the end, you should be able to design reusable base classes, implement required behaviors in derived classes, and avoid common pitfalls like object slicing or forgetting to mark functions virtual. Which part of your current project might become a clean base class?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Inheritance & Polymorphism
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Inheritance & Polymorphism

Build hierarchies that capture shared behavior, and use virtual functions so the engine dispatches the correct implementation at runtime. We focus on C++ patterns that Unreal expects, like virtual, pure virtual, and override.

Why this matters

Cleaner code, fewer bugs, and the ability to treat many objects through a single interface.

Practical payoff

A single manager can call Fire() or Attack() on any derived object and get the right behavior automatically.

Explore Key Topics
Inheritance
Reuse fields and functions by deriving AZombieEnemy from AEnemy.
Polymorphism
Call Attack() on AEnemy* pointers and get derived behavior at runtime.
Abstract interfaces
Use pure virtual functions to force derived classes to implement required methods.
Concept map
AEnemy (base)
Health, MovementSpeed, virtual Attack()
AZombieEnemy
Overrides Attack(), implements TakeDamage()
ASpiderEnemy
Different Attack() behavior, same interface
Tip: favor pointers or references when you want polymorphic behavior. Passing derived objects by value causes slicing and loses derived identity.
Key Takeaway

Design a base class to capture shared rules, use virtual and pure virtual functions to define replaceable or required behavior, and apply override to avoid mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately in Unreal C++ development. First, you'll understand inheritance: how to create a new class from an existing one to share properties and behavior, and why that reduces duplication. Second, you'll apply polymorphism to build systems where managers operate on base-class pointers while concrete types provide specific implementations at runtime. Third, you'll differentiate virtual and pure virtual functions: virtual enables runtime selection while pure virtual makes a class abstract and enforces implementation in derived types. Fourth, you'll implement and override virtual functions in Unreal C++ classes and use the override keyword to help the compiler catch mismatches. Each objective combines a conceptual definition and a practical reason to care, so you can both design clean hierarchies and avoid common mistakes during implementation.

screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance means creating a new class based on an existing one so the new class automatically gets the fields and functions from its parent. In game development you commonly define a base actor such as AEnemy that holds shared properties like Health and MovementSpeed, then derive AZombieEnemy or ADragonEnemy that extend or modify behavior. This reduces duplicated code: common logic lives once in the base and specialized logic lives in derived classes. A derived class 'is-a' base class: an AZombieEnemy is an AEnemy, so anywhere the engine expects an AEnemy you can use a zombie. A practical example: put common damage handling and movement code in AEnemy, and let derived classes change only the animations or attack pattern. A common misconception is thinking inheritance is only for reuse; it's also a modeling tool for domain relationships. But avoid deep inheritance chains for every variation—prefer composition when behavior changes are orthogonal. To check understanding, imagine your game has many pickup types; ask whether their common code should be in a base collectible class or split into separate components. The core insight: inheritance groups shared state and behavior so your codebase remains organized and extensible.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets derived classes reuse and specialize behavior declared in a base class, expressing an 'is-a' relationship.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is Inheritance?
Core Concept

Reuse and model relationships

Inheritance groups common fields and functionality into a base class so derived classes build on that shared foundation.

Example
AEnemy defines Health and TakeDamage(); AZombieEnemy inherits those and adds bite behavior.
Misconception
Inheritance is not only for code reuse — it's for modeling 'is-a' relationships. Use composition if the relationship is not hierarchical.
Key Takeaway

Organize shared behavior in base classes and keep derived classes focused on specialization to improve maintainability.

Class Hierarchy Example
UObject
AActor
ACharacter
Concrete example:
AEnemy (base)
  • Properties: Health, MovementSpeed
  • Functions: virtual Attack(), virtual TakeDamage(float)
AZombieEnemy — overrides Attack()
ADragonEnemy — overrides Attack(), adds Fire()

screens.title: Unreal Class Hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's built-in class hierarchy is an instructive example of inheritance in practice. At the top sits UObject; AActor inherits from it and adds actor-level behavior, and ACharacter further extends AActor with movement and animation systems. When you create a custom actor or character, you pick the appropriate base class so you inherit engine functionality immediately. This means that lifecycle hooks already declared as virtual—like BeginPlay, Tick, and PostInitializeComponents—are available for you to override safely. The significance is twofold: first, selecting the correct base class gives you useful default behavior; second, because these functions are virtual, your overrides are invoked correctly by the engine at runtime. A practical pitfall is deriving from a class that lacks the functionality you need; pick the minimal base that provides required behavior. For example, if you need character movement and input, inherit ACharacter. If you only need a passive actor, derive from AActor. This architecture lesson helps you make the right inheritance choices and understand why lifecycle virtuals exist in the engine. Unreal Class Hierarchy means choose the appropriate unreal base class to inherit engine behavior; built-in virtual lifecycle functions let derived classes inject custom logic.. In practical terms, how aactor, acharacter, and your classes relate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Unreal Class Hierarchy
Architecture

Engine hierarchy: UObject → AActor → ACharacter

Each layer adds features. AActor provides scene presence and lifecycle events; ACharacter adds movement and animation systems you can immediately reuse.

UObject — base for all UE objects
AActor — actor lifecycle, replication, components
ACharacter — movement, input-ready, character-specific components
Why it matters
Picking the right base class gives you engine features you would otherwise reimplement and ensures virtual lifecycle functions are available to override.
Lifecycle examples
BeginPlay() — initialization when play begins; often overridden in derived actors
Tick(float DeltaTime) — per-frame updates; override to update behavior every frame
PostInitializeComponents() — component setup; sometimes used for component-driven initialization
Misconception: You don't need to re-declare BeginPlay() as virtual; the base class already declares it virtual so your override will be called. The important step is to use the correct signature and optionally call Super::BeginPlay().

screens.title: Polymorphism Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism allows objects of different derived types to be used where a base type is expected, and for the correct derived behavior to run at runtime. In Unreal C++ this typically means holding pointers or references to a base class—AEnemy* or AWeapon*—and calling virtual functions. The runtime determines which override to call based on the actual object type, not the pointer type. A concrete example: place AZombieEnemy and ASpiderEnemy instances into a TArray and then loop, calling Attack() on each element. Each enemy runs its own Attack() method: zombie bite, spider venom. This eliminates sprawling if-else chains or type checks, and it lets you add new enemy types without changing the code that uses them. A frequent misconception is expecting polymorphism to work when objects are passed by value; this causes object slicing and loses the derived portion. Always use pointers or references for polymorphic objects. As a reflective question, consider: where in your game could a manager call a single function across many types and benefit from polymorphism? That is a sign a base interface will simplify your design.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism
keyIdea.text: Treat many concrete types as their base type and rely on virtual functions to dispatch the correct behavior at runtime.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Polymorphism Explained
Definition

Many forms from one interface

Use base-class pointers so code can invoke derived behavior without knowing the concrete type.

Concrete example: TArray<AEnemy*> filled with AZombieEnemy and ASpiderEnemy; calling Attack() dispatches correctly for each object.
Misconception: Passing by value slices derived data; use pointers or references for polymorphism.
Key Takeaway

Polymorphism reduces coupling: add new derived types without changing the code that uses the base interface.

Quick checklist
  • Use pointers or references for polymorphic storage.
  • Mark the base function virtual to enable dynamic dispatch.
  • Prefer override in derived implementations for safety.
  • Avoid object slicing by not passing polymorphic objects by value.

screens.title: Virtual vs Pure Virtual Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Virtual and pure virtual functions serve different design goals. A virtual function in a base class provides a default implementation but allows derived classes to override it. This is useful when the base behavior is reasonable for most derived types but some types need different behavior. A pure virtual function, declared with equals zero, makes the base class abstract and requires every concrete derived class to provide an implementation. Use pure virtual when the base cannot reasonably define a default; for example, TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) might be pure virtual on AEnemy to force each enemy type to implement how damage affects them. A common error is making a function non-virtual when you intend derived types to replace it; that leads to function hiding where base-class calls always run the base implementation. Another error is trying to instantiate an abstract class—compilers will stop you when pure virtuals exist. Both constructs are tools: pick virtual for optional customization and pure virtual to define required interface contracts. As a practice check, ask whether the base class can provide a sensible default; if not, declare the function pure virtual so derived classes must implement the required behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Virtual vs Pure Virtual
Comparison

Virtual vs Pure Virtual

Virtual: Base provides a default and derived types may override.
Pure virtual (= 0): No base implementation; derived classes must implement it, making the base abstract.
Example: virtual void Attack(); versus virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) = 0;
Guidelines
  • Use virtual when the base can supply a useful fallback behavior.
  • Use pure virtual to define an interface that every derived class must implement.
  • Remember pure virtual classes cannot be instantiated directly; they act as abstract interfaces.
Common mistake: forgetting virtual means calls through base pointers invoke the base implementation always, breaking polymorphism.

screens.title: Using override and implementing virtuals
screens.narratorSegment: The override keyword is a defensive practice in modern C++. When you write override in a derived-class method signature, you tell the compiler you expect to override a base virtual method. If the signature does not match—for example you mistype a parameter—the compiler raises an error. This prevents bugs where your method silently hides the base function instead of overriding it. In Unreal C++ you commonly declare functions with UFUNCTION macro and then mark their C++ signature with override in the derived header. For example, AZombieEnemy declares virtual void Attack() override to show intent. A concrete example from the chapter: AEnemy declares virtual void Attack(); AZombieEnemy implements virtual void Attack() override; and the compiler verifies the override. Always prefer override when your derived method should supply a replacement implementation. A misconception is thinking override changes runtime behavior; it only affects compile-time checks. The runtime still uses virtual dispatch. Your practical checklist: use virtual in the base where appropriate, use override in derived types, and compile frequently to catch signature mismatches early. Using override and implementing virtuals means always mark derived implementations with override so the compiler verifies you actually override a virtual base function.. In practical terms, compiler-assisted correctness with the override keyword. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Use override
Code Walkthrough

Override for safety

Use override so the compiler catches signature mismatches and prevents accidental function hiding.

// Enemy.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AEnemy : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    virtual void Attack();
    virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) = 0; // Pure virtual
};

// ZombieEnemy.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AZombieEnemy : public AEnemy
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    virtual void Attack() override; // Compiler checks this matches base
    virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) override;
};
Practical note
override is compile-time help. It does not change dynamic dispatch semantics, but it avoids subtle, hard-to-find bugs caused by typos or signature mismatches.
Check
When a derived method intends to replace a base virtual, include override on the signature and compile to confirm.

screens.title: AEnemy, AZombieEnemy: Attack and TakeDamage
screens.narratorSegment: Let's step through a concrete example from the chapter to see how virtual and pure virtual functions are used in practice. At runtime, storing pointers to AEnemy in a TArray allows you to call Attack() polymorphically for every enemy type in that array, with each class's override executed. This example highlights three practical points: use pure virtual to require essential methods, use override for compiler verification, and always store polymorphic objects via pointers or references to avoid slicing. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › AEnemy → AZombieEnemy
Code Example
// Enemy.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AEnemy : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AEnemy();
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
    virtual void Attack();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
    virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) = 0; // Pure virtual
};

// ZombieEnemy.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AZombieEnemy : public AEnemy
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AZombieEnemy();
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
    virtual void Attack() override; 

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
    virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) override;

screens.title: Mistakes that break polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes that cause polymorphism to fail in practice. The first is forgetting to mark a base-class function as virtual. If a derived class defines a function with the same name but the base didn't declare it virtual, calls through base pointers invoke the base method and you lose polymorphic behavior. The second is object slicing: passing a derived object by value to a function that expects a base object copies only the base portion, discarding derived state and vtable identity. This removes polymorphism entirely. The third is attempting to instantiate an abstract class that contains one or more pure virtual functions; the compiler will block this because the abstract class lacks concrete implementations. Finally, mismatched signatures or forgotten override annotations can hide errors. To avoid these pitfalls, always use pointers or references for polymorphism, mark intended overridable functions as virtual in the base, use pure virtuals when forcing implementation, and mark derived functions with override to let the compiler check your intent. Reflect: inspect your code for any base-function declarations missing virtual that should be overrideable.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Common Pitfalls
Troubleshooting

Why polymorphism may break

  • Forgetting virtual in the base function — calls use base implementation always.
  • Object slicing — passing derived by value loses derived parts.
  • Attempting to instantiate an abstract class with pure virtuals — compiler error.
  • Signature mismatches — derived method hides base if signatures differ.
Fix checklist
- Store polymorphic objects as pointers or references.
- Mark overridable base methods with virtual.
- Use override in derived methods for safety.
- Use pure virtual to enforce required implementations.
Common misconception: thinking copy semantics preserve polymorphism. Remember: copies of base type lose derived identity.

screens.title: Lifecycle functions and overriding
screens.narratorSegment: Many Unreal lifecycle functions are declared virtual in engine base classes so derived classes may provide custom logic that the engine executes at the right time. BeginPlay() is called once when an actor enters play; Tick(float DeltaTime) runs every frame; PostInitializeComponents() runs after component initialization; EndPlay() runs when an actor is removed. Because these functions are virtual, you override them in your derived classes to inject initialization, per-frame updates, component hookup, or cleanup. A common pattern is to override BeginPlay(), call Super::BeginPlay() to retain base behavior, and then add your actor-specific setup. This design allows the engine to operate on base-class pointers but still execute concrete behaviors implemented in derived classes. One misconception is that you must re-declare BeginPlay() as virtual in your derived header; you do not—the function is already virtual. The important part is matching the signature and, when needed, marking override so the compiler can validate your intent. Ultimately, lifecycle virtuals make the engine extensible by design. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Lifecycle Overrides
Integration

Override engine lifecycle safely

BeginPlay(): initialization when play starts. Override to set up state and spawn dependent actors. Call Super::BeginPlay().
Tick(float DeltaTime): per-frame updates for movement, timers, or procedural behavior.
PostInitializeComponents(): use for component-dependent initialization after components are created.
Practical rules
  • Match the signature exactly when overriding.
  • Use override so the compiler checks you actually override a virtual function.
  • Call Super::... when you want to preserve base class behavior as well.
Why it matters: lifecycle virtuals allow the engine to call your class-specific logic without knowing the concrete type of every actor.

screens.title: Designing Base Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Designing base interfaces is a deliberate choice: decide which behaviors every derived class must implement and which can have default implementations. If every derived type must perform an action—for example, all collectible items must implement Collect()—declare it pure virtual in the base so the compiler enforces it. If most types share reasonable behavior, provide a virtual default in the base and allow selective overrides. Abstract classes (with pure virtuals) are ideal for interface-style bases that have no standalone meaning; they prevent instantiation of incomplete types. For example, create ACollectibleItem with virtual void Collect() = 0 so ACoin and AHealthPotion implement their own collection effects. Avoid putting too many responsibilities into a single base class; prefer small interfaces and composition for orthogonal behaviors. A practical test: if you cannot sensibly construct a meaningful base object on its own, consider making it abstract. This keeps your hierarchy clear about required behavior and reduces accidental misuse. Designing Base Interfaces means make base classes abstract to enforce required methods; provide defaults when a common behavior exists that most derived types will share.. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Designing Interfaces
Definition & Advice

Abstract vs default behaviour

Abstract base (pure virtual): forces derived classes to implement the required functionality.
Default virtual: provides common logic, derived types can override to specialize.
Example: ACollectibleItem::Collect() = 0 forces each pick-up to specify its collection effect.
Design checklist
  • Can the base be meaningfully instantiated? If no, consider making it abstract.
  • Is there a common default for most types? If yes, provide a virtual implementation.
  • Prefer small focused interfaces and composition over large monolithic bases.
Quick thought experiment: if you cannot create a useful object from the base alone, make the base abstract to prevent accidental usage.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll see how inheritance and polymorphism form the backbone of extendable game systems in Unreal Engine. We use inheritance to express “is-a” relationships: a zombie is an enemy, a character is an actor. That gives derived types automatic access to fields and behaviors defined in a base class, reducing duplication and organizing code. Polymorphism lets code treat many concrete types through a single interface. Using virtual functions, the engine will call the appropriate derived implementation at runtime, so a single loop over an array of base-class pointers triggers zombie attacks, spider bites, or dragon fire without explicit type checks. You will also learn the difference between virtual and pure virtual functions, why an abstract base class enforces an interface, and why the override keyword prevents subtle bugs. Practical examples in this chapter build an AWeapon base class and ARifle/APistol derived classes, plus a WeaponManager that demonstrates calling Fire() polymorphically. By the end, you should be able to design reusable base classes, implement required behaviors in derived classes, and avoid common pitfalls like object slicing or forgetting to mark functions virtual. Which part of your current project might become a clean base class?

These learning objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately in Unreal C++ development. First, you'll understand inheritance: how to create a new class from an existing one to share properties and behavior, and why that reduces duplication. Second, you'll apply polymorphism to build systems where managers operate on base-class pointers while concrete types provide specific implementations at runtime. Third, you'll differentiate virtual and pure virtual functions: virtual enables runtime selection while pure virtual makes a class abstract and enforces implementation in derived types. Fourth, you'll implement and override virtual functions in Unreal C++ classes and use the override keyword to help the compiler catch mismatches. Each objective combines a conceptual definition and a practical reason to care, so you can both design clean hierarchies and avoid common mistakes during implementation.

These additional objectives focus on practical application and safe design. First, you will recognize common pitfalls like forgetting to mark a function virtual, which defeats polymorphism, or accidentally instantiating an abstract class. Second, you'll learn to use Unreal lifecycle virtual functions—BeginPlay, Tick—safely so your custom logic runs in derived classes. Third, you will design base class interfaces with pure virtual functions to require derived implementations, ensuring every derived object supports the same contract. Finally, you will complete the hands-on activity: create AWeapon with virtual Fire(), derive ARifle and APistol that override Fire(), then use a WeaponManager to call Fire() polymorphically. These objectives ensure not only conceptual understanding but also practical ability to implement and test polymorphic behavior in an Unreal project. In practical terms, apply patterns and avoid common inheritance pitfalls. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inheritance means creating a new class based on an existing one so the new class automatically gets the fields and functions from its parent. In game development you commonly define a base actor such as AEnemy that holds shared properties like Health and MovementSpeed, then derive AZombieEnemy or ADragonEnemy that extend or modify behavior. This reduces duplicated code: common logic lives once in the base and specialized logic lives in derived classes. A derived class 'is-a' base class: an AZombieEnemy is an AEnemy, so anywhere the engine expects an AEnemy you can use a zombie. A practical example: put common damage handling and movement code in AEnemy, and let derived classes change only the animations or attack pattern. A common misconception is thinking inheritance is only for reuse; it's also a modeling tool for domain relationships. But avoid deep inheritance chains for every variation—prefer composition when behavior changes are orthogonal. To check understanding, imagine your game has many pickup types; ask whether their common code should be in a base collectible class or split into separate components. The core insight: inheritance groups shared state and behavior so your codebase remains organized and extensible.

Unreal's built-in class hierarchy is an instructive example of inheritance in practice. At the top sits UObject; AActor inherits from it and adds actor-level behavior, and ACharacter further extends AActor with movement and animation systems. When you create a custom actor or character, you pick the appropriate base class so you inherit engine functionality immediately. This means that lifecycle hooks already declared as virtual—like BeginPlay, Tick, and PostInitializeComponents—are available for you to override safely. The significance is twofold: first, selecting the correct base class gives you useful default behavior; second, because these functions are virtual, your overrides are invoked correctly by the engine at runtime. A practical pitfall is deriving from a class that lacks the functionality you need; pick the minimal base that provides required behavior. For example, if you need character movement and input, inherit ACharacter. If you only need a passive actor, derive from AActor. This architecture lesson helps you make the right inheritance choices and understand why lifecycle virtuals exist in the engine. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Polymorphism allows objects of different derived types to be used where a base type is expected, and for the correct derived behavior to run at runtime. In Unreal C++ this typically means holding pointers or references to a base class—AEnemy* or AWeapon*—and calling virtual functions. The runtime determines which override to call based on the actual object type, not the pointer type. A concrete example: place AZombieEnemy and ASpiderEnemy instances into a TArray and then loop, calling Attack() on each element. Each enemy runs its own Attack() method: zombie bite, spider venom. This eliminates sprawling if-else chains or type checks, and it lets you add new enemy types without changing the code that uses them. A frequent misconception is expecting polymorphism to work when objects are passed by value; this causes object slicing and loses the derived portion. Always use pointers or references for polymorphic objects. As a reflective question, consider: where in your game could a manager call a single function across many types and benefit from polymorphism? That is a sign a base interface will simplify your design.

Virtual and pure virtual functions serve different design goals. A virtual function in a base class provides a default implementation but allows derived classes to override it. This is useful when the base behavior is reasonable for most derived types but some types need different behavior. A pure virtual function, declared with equals zero, makes the base class abstract and requires every concrete derived class to provide an implementation. Use pure virtual when the base cannot reasonably define a default; for example, TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) might be pure virtual on AEnemy to force each enemy type to implement how damage affects them. A common error is making a function non-virtual when you intend derived types to replace it; that leads to function hiding where base-class calls always run the base implementation. Another error is trying to instantiate an abstract class—compilers will stop you when pure virtuals exist. Both constructs are tools: pick virtual for optional customization and pure virtual to define required interface contracts. As a practice check, ask whether the base class can provide a sensible default; if not, declare the function pure virtual so derived classes must implement the required behavior.

The override keyword is a defensive practice in modern C++. When you write override in a derived-class method signature, you tell the compiler you expect to override a base virtual method. If the signature does not match—for example you mistype a parameter—the compiler raises an error. This prevents bugs where your method silently hides the base function instead of overriding it. In Unreal C++ you commonly declare functions with UFUNCTION macro and then mark their C++ signature with override in the derived header. For example, AZombieEnemy declares virtual void Attack() override to show intent. A concrete example from the chapter: AEnemy declares virtual void Attack(); AZombieEnemy implements virtual void Attack() override; and the compiler verifies the override. Always prefer override when your derived method should supply a replacement implementation. A misconception is thinking override changes runtime behavior; it only affects compile-time checks. The runtime still uses virtual dispatch. Your practical checklist: use virtual in the base where appropriate, use override in derived types, and compile frequently to catch signature mismatches early. Using override and implementing virtuals means always mark derived implementations with override so the compiler verifies you actually override a virtual base function.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are a few recurring mistakes that cause polymorphism to fail in practice. The first is forgetting to mark a base-class function as virtual. If a derived class defines a function with the same name but the base didn't declare it virtual, calls through base pointers invoke the base method and you lose polymorphic behavior. The second is object slicing: passing a derived object by value to a function that expects a base object copies only the base portion, discarding derived state and vtable identity. This removes polymorphism entirely. The third is attempting to instantiate an abstract class that contains one or more pure virtual functions; the compiler will block this because the abstract class lacks concrete implementations. Finally, mismatched signatures or forgotten override annotations can hide errors. To avoid these pitfalls, always use pointers or references for polymorphism, mark intended overridable functions as virtual in the base, use pure virtuals when forcing implementation, and mark derived functions with override to let the compiler check your intent. Many Unreal lifecycle functions are declared virtual in engine base classes so derived classes may provide custom logic that the engine executes at the right time. BeginPlay() is called once when an actor enters play; Tick(float DeltaTime) runs every frame; PostInitializeComponents() runs after component initialization; EndPlay() runs when an actor is removed. Because these functions are virtual, you override them in your derived classes to inject initialization, per-frame updates, component hookup, or cleanup. A common pattern is to override BeginPlay(), call Super::BeginPlay() to retain base behavior, and then add your actor-specific setup. This design allows the engine to operate on base-class pointers but still execute concrete behaviors implemented in derived classes. One misconception is that you must re-declare BeginPlay() as virtual in your derived header; you do not—the function is already virtual. The important part is matching the signature and, when needed, marking override so the compiler can validate your intent. Ultimately, lifecycle virtuals make the engine extensible by design. Designing base interfaces is a deliberate choice: decide which behaviors every derived class must implement and which can have default implementations. If every derived type must perform an action—for example, all collectible items must implement Collect()—declare it pure virtual in the base so the compiler enforces it. If most types share reasonable behavior, provide a virtual default in the base and allow selective overrides. Abstract classes (with pure virtuals) are ideal for interface-style bases that have no standalone meaning; they prevent instantiation of incomplete types. For example, create ACollectibleItem with virtual void Collect() = 0 so ACoin and AHealthPotion implement their own collection effects. Avoid putting too many responsibilities into a single base class; prefer small interfaces and composition for orthogonal behaviors. A practical test: if you cannot sensibly construct a meaningful base object on its own, consider making it abstract. This keeps your hierarchy clear about required behavior and reduces accidental misuse. Let's recap the most important ideas from this chapter. First, inheritance groups shared state and functionality so derived classes focus on specialization. Second, polymorphism, enabled by virtual functions, lets a single interface drive many concrete behaviors at runtime without type checks. Third, pure virtual functions define abstract interfaces that force derived types to implement required methods. Fourth, the override keyword is your compile-time guard against signature mismatches. Finally, avoid common traps: missing virtual, object slicing, and attempting to instantiate abstract classes. Keep these concepts in mind as you design base classes and managers; they will make your code more modular and easier to extend.
